stumbles.why: Refers to earlier work between Oskar and the author that the text never describes.

stumbles.quote: its main use for remex would be faster training
stumbles.why: remex is never explained (apparently a quantization/search library); we can't tell what it is or what it trains.
Unexplained prior system; unclear what the quantizer is, how it's applied per dimension, or what the baseline is.

stumbles.quote: e-means reaches the error of 25 iterations of Lloyd's k-means in 1 to 3 passes
stumbles.why: e-means is never described. 'Passes' is not defined, and it's unclear whether a pass is comparable to a Lloyd iteration.

stumbles.quote: On 4 CPUs that is 1.6 to 10.2 times sooner.
stumbles.why: Unclear whether the speedup is wall-clock or iterations, and which pass count maps to which speedup. The baseline and k are not given.

stumbles.quote: the centroid table costs 126 bytes per vector
stumbles.why: This doesn't follow from the text. 4,096 centroids over 100,000 vectors is amortised, and the dimension and precision are not given. It is also compared to a second bit per dimension with no figure for that cost.

stumbles.quote: remex's hash cells find 70% while scanning 34%.
stumbles.why: The hash-cell method is not explained. The comparison also isn't like for like: the 90% recall is of 'true neighbours' with no stated k, whereas the earlier figure was recall@10.

stumbles.quote: A search that scans 0.56% of the corpus finds 90% of the true neighbours.
stumbles.why: 0.56% of the corpus is about 1/178, but with 4,096 cells a single cell would be about 0.024%. The number of cells probed (nprobe) is never given, so the scan fraction can't be reproduced.

stumbles.quote: I had expected the offset coding to be the result and the index cells to be a side note; it came out the other way.
stumbles.why: This conflicts with the earlier statement that the expected main use was faster training. Which expectation was real is unclear.

point: Using 4,096 k-means centroids as index cells (IVF-style) reached 90% recall while scanning only 0.56% of the corpus, which is far better than the author's hash cells. This mattered more than the faster e-means training or the offset coding, and Lloyd and e-means centroids give the same recall.
